pos: n. (the Palatinate capital on the Neckar, whose university produced the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563)
etymology: German Heidelberg, probably the hill of the bilberry or the heath hill, from Heidelbeere or Heide with Berg, a hill.
biblical_def: Heidelberg on the Neckar was the capital of the Electoral Palatinate and the seat of the oldest university in Germany, founded in 1386. Luther disputed there in 1518 and set out in the Heidelberg Disputation the theology of the cross against the theology of glory. The Palatinate went Lutheran, then under Frederick III, who succeeded in 1559, turned Reformed; he commissioned Zacharias Ursinus and Caspar Olevianus to draw up a catechism, and the Heidelberg Catechism was published in 1563 and has been the most widely loved of all the Reformed catechisms since. Its first question asks what a man's only comfort in life and death is, and its answer begins with belonging to Christ. The Thirty Years War wrecked the city and the Palatine library was carted off to Rome in 1623. The dictionary records Heidelberg for the Catechism, and the Catechism for its order: it treats sin, then salvation, then service, and it puts justification where Paul puts it, as a gift received by faith and never a wage, so that no man has anything left to boast of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited favour of God; faith as belief in the testimony of God; a gift as something bestowed freely; to boast as to vaunt oneself; and to justify as to pronounce righteous.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favor; good will; kindness; the free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence renewing the heart.
FAITH, n. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what God reveals, resting on his authority and veracity; evangelical faith.
GIFT, n. A present; any thing given or bestowed; the act of bestowing; a bribe; a faculty bestowed by God.
BOAST, v.i. To brag, or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display of one's own worth or actions.
JUSTIFY, v.t. To pronounce free from guilt or blame; in theology, to pardon and clear from guilt, and to accept as righteous.
corruption_summary: Palatinate capital and university city on the Neckar, where Luther disputed in 1518 and where Ursinus and Olevianus wrote the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Catechism keeps in its right place. Paul leaves no room for a contribution: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and he states the consequence as the reason for the arrangement, “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9).

The live temptation is to concede the doctrine and then teach something else to children, which is exactly what a catechism exists to prevent. Paul's summary is a conclusion drawn from an argument and not a slogan: “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). Instruction of the young is the ordinary means by which such a conclusion survives a generation, and the promise attached to it is explicit: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). Heidelberg wrote its doctrine into questions a child could answer.

pos: n. (the Swabian imperial city of the Diet of 1530, the Interim of 1548 and the Peace of 1555)
etymology: German Augsburg, from the Roman Augusta Vindelicorum, the Augustan city of the Vindelici.
biblical_def: Augsburg was a free imperial city on the Lech, rich on the banking of the Fugger family, and three of the decisive events of the German Reformation happened in it. In 1518 Luther was examined there by Cajetan and refused to recant. In 1530 the Diet of Augsburg received the Augsburg Confession, drawn up by Melanchthon and read aloud in German before Charles V by the Saxon chancellor, which remains the chief Lutheran confession. In 1548, after the emperor's victory, the Augsburg Interim was imposed, restoring most of the old worship and splitting the Lutherans over how much could be conceded in things indifferent. In 1555 the Peace of Augsburg ended the fighting on the principle that each prince would settle the religion of his own territory. The dictionary records Augsburg for the reading of the Confession. Men put their names to a document before an emperor who could destroy them, which is the plain apostolic duty: whoever confesses Christ before men will be confessed before the Father, and we ought to obey God rather than men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to confess as to own and acknowledge openly; a confession as an avowal of faith; to obey as to comply with authority; to contend as to strive earnestly; and to exhort as to urge by argument.
webster_full: CONFESS, v.t. To own, acknowledge or avow; to acknowledge faith in or obedience to; to profess openly.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or debt; avowal; a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
OBEY, v.t. To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior; to submit to the government of.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive; to struggle in opposition; to dispute earnestly; to strive in debate.
EXHORT, v.t. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct.
corruption_summary: Swabian imperial city of Luther's 1518 examination, the Augsburg Confession of 1530, the Interim of 1548 and the Peace of 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that confession is a public act performed where it costs something. Christ attaches his own acknowledgment to it: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32). When the apostles were forbidden to speak, they gave the ruling that every Augsburg delegate needed, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

The live temptation at Augsburg was the Interim, which asked men to concede ceremonies as indifferent and then found that the concessions were the point; the quarrel it caused among the Lutherans lasted twenty years. Jude requires contention for a fixed deposit, not for a negotiable position: believers are to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). And the duty does not pause for a bad political season: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (the great Rhineland archbishopric, where Hermann von Wied's attempted Reformation was crushed in 1546)
etymology: From Latin Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, shortened to Colonia; German Köln, French Cologne.
biblical_def: Cologne was the largest city in Germany through the Middle Ages, an archbishopric whose holder was one of the seven electors, and the most determinedly conservative church centre in the empire; its university condemned Luther in 1519, Tyndale's first printing of the English New Testament was broken up there in 1525, and its relics of the Three Kings drew pilgrims from all Europe to a cathedral that stood unfinished with a crane on its stump for three hundred years. Against that background Hermann von Wied, archbishop from 1515, grew convinced of the Reformation, brought in Bucer and Melanchthon in 1542 to draft a reforming order for his province, and was excommunicated and deposed by 1547, his clergy and university having fought him throughout. The dictionary records Cologne for the resistance rather than the attempt. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that the opposition would rise from inside the ministry itself, and he foretold a time when men would not endure sound doctrine but would prefer teachers chosen to suit them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sound as whole and uncorrupted; doctrine as that which is taught; to endure as to bear with patience; perverse as obstinately wrong; and a teacher as one who instructs.
webster_full: SOUND, a. Entire; unbroken; not shaky or decayed; healthy; founded in truth; firm; valid; orthodox.
DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principles or positions in any science; the truths of the gospel in general.
ENDURE, v.t. To bear; to sustain; to support without breaking or yielding; to undergo; to tolerate.
PERVERSE, a. Literally, turned aside; hence, distorted from the right; obstinate in the wrong; stubborn.
TEACHER, n. One who teaches or instructs; an instructor; a preceptor; one who instructs others in religion.
corruption_summary: Largest German city and an electoral archbishopric, whose clergy and university defeated Archbishop Hermann von Wied's attempted Reformation by 1547.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's warning about the source of the worst opposition, which is not outside the church: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). He describes the appetite that makes such men successful, that the time will come “when they will not endure sound doctrine” (2Ti 4:3).

The live temptation at Cologne was a prosperous religion with everything to lose, a cathedral full of relics, a university with a reputation, and a clergy with incomes, all of it mobilised against its own archbishop. The qualification Paul requires of an overseer is competence in the deposit rather than in the politics: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). And the duty of testing falls on ordinary believers as well: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1). Hermann von Wied was deposed; the New Testament he could not stop printing was printed in Worms.

pos: n. (the primatial see of Germany, Boniface's city, where Gutenberg printed and whose archbishop licensed the indulgence that provoked Luther)
etymology: From the Roman Mogontiacum, a Celtic name; German Mainz, English formerly Mayence.
biblical_def: Mainz, where the Main joins the Rhine, was the primatial see of Germany from the eighth century, its archbishop an elector and arch-chancellor of the empire. Boniface held it, Rabanus Maurus taught there, and in the 1450s Johannes Gutenberg printed in it the forty-two-line Bible, the first substantial book produced with movable type in Europe, which within fifty years had made printed Scripture ordinary and made the Reformation technically possible. The same see supplied the occasion of the Reformation: Albrecht of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz from 1514, owed enormous sums for his accumulated offices and licensed Tetzel's indulgence preaching in his province to repay them, which is what Luther's theses attacked. The dictionary records Mainz for holding both ends of the story. A press in that city made the text available and an indulgence sold in that province made its doctrine urgent. Scripture had already given the instruction to write plainly for a running reader, and the doctrine the press then spread is that a man is not justified by the works of the law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to print as to take an impression; plain as clear and evident; the law as a rule prescribed by authority; justified as pronounced righteous; and to prosper as to succeed.
webster_full: PRINT, v.t. To take or form an impression of letters or figures by means of types; to publish; to impress.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure or difficult; open; artless.
LAW, n. A rule prescribed by authority; the moral law contained in the ten commandments; the Mosaic ritual.
JUSTIFIED, pp. Pardoned and accepted as righteous; freed from the imputation of guilt; vindicated.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to thrive; to make gain or increase; to flourish.
corruption_summary: Primatial German see held by Boniface, where Gutenberg printed the first European Bible with movable type and whose archbishop licensed the indulgence Luther attacked.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture itself asks to be made legible and portable. The LORD'S own instruction to a prophet anticipates a press: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). What Gutenberg's Bible then carried to every university in Europe is the sentence that undid the indulgence trade in that same province: “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16).

The live temptation at Mainz was simony dressed as finance, an archbishop borrowing to buy offices and selling pardon to service the debt, with the people charged for both. The remedy was not a better accounting but a text, and Paul states what it reveals: “therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith” (Rom 1:17). The errand of such a word is guaranteed by the one who sends it: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

pos: n. (the Rhineland imperial city of the Diet of 1521, where Luther refused to recant, and of the 1527 Prophets translation)
etymology: From the Celtic Borbetomagus through Latin Wormatia; the German Worms keeps the later form.
biblical_def: Worms on the Rhine was one of the oldest imperial cities and the seat of more than a hundred imperial diets. At the Diet of Worms in April 1521 Luther was brought before Charles V, shown his books, and asked whether he would retract them; he asked for a day, and on 18 April answered that unless he were convinced by Scripture or plain reason he could not and would not recant, since to act against conscience is neither safe nor honest. The Edict of Worms outlawed him. Worms remained a Protestant stronghold; in 1527 Hans Denck and Ludwig Haetzer printed there the first German translation of the Prophets from Hebrew, which Luther used, and the city held one of the oldest Jewish communities in Germany and the oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in Europe. The dictionary records Worms for 18 April 1521, and for what Luther appealed to. He did not claim a private illumination; he asked to be shown a text, and the compulsion he described is the one Jeremiah knew, a word in the heart as a burning fire that could not be kept in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the moral sense judging right and wrong; to recant as to retract a declaration; a testimony as a solemn declaration; to be ashamed as to be confounded; and a word as that which is spoken or written.
webster_full: CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
RECANT, v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to take back what has been said.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing some fact; witness; the precepts of God.
ASHAMED, a. Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt or a conviction of some impropriety.
WORD, n. An articulate sound used as the sign of an idea; in the plural, the Scriptures; a promise.
corruption_summary: Rhineland imperial city where Luther refused to recant before Charles V in April 1521, and where the first German translation of the Prophets from Hebrew was printed in 1527.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the nature of the compulsion Luther described, which Scripture had already put in a prophet's mouth. Jeremiah tried to stop speaking and could not: “But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9). The apostles before the council put the matter to their judges as a question of competing authority, “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).

The live temptation is to read Worms as a defence of conscience in general, which it was not. Luther offered to be refuted from Scripture and asked for nothing else, and the apostles' ground is the same, a thing seen and heard rather than a right to self-expression: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20). The Psalmist had long since described the posture of a man with a text in front of an emperor: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46).

pos: n. (the city on the Rhine at the lake, where the council of 1414 burned Hus, and which was Protestant from 1527 until 1548)
etymology: From Latin Constantia, named for the emperor Constantius; German Konstanz.
biblical_def: Constance stands where the Rhine leaves the lake that bears its name, and it was the seat of the largest medieval bishopric north of the Alps. The Council of Constance met there from 1414 to 1418, ended the papal schism by deposing or accepting the resignation of three claimants, condemned the writings of Wyclif, and dealt with Jan Hus, who had come under an imperial safe-conduct from Sigismund, was imprisoned on arrival, refused to abjure articles he said were not his, and was burned on 6 July 1415; Jerome of Prague followed him in 1416. The breaking of the safe-conduct was defended on the ground that no faith need be kept with a heretic. A century later the city itself turned Protestant under Ambrosius Blarer and Johannes Zwick, held out through the 1530s, and was forced back to the old religion by Charles V in 1548 and placed under Austria. The dictionary records Constance for the fire and the safe-conduct. Scripture says the death of God's saints is precious in his sight, and it promises rest and a following record to those who die in the Lord.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; precious as of great value; to rest as to cease from labour; a witness as one who gives testimony; and faithful as firm in adherence to the truth.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who suffers death in defense of any belief.
PRECIOUS, a. Of great price; costly; of great value or worth; very valuable; highly esteemed.
REST, v.i. To cease from action or motion of any kind; to be quiet or still; to sleep; to lie in death.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; one who sees or knows a thing and can testify to it.
FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to allegiance; constant in affection.
corruption_summary: Rhine city of the Council of 1414-18, which burned Hus in 1415 under a broken safe-conduct; Protestant from 1527 until forced back by Charles V in 1548.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the value God sets on such a death, which no council can lower: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15). John is told to write it down as a beatitude with a reason attached, “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth” (Rev 14:13).

The live temptation at Constance was the one the council yielded to, which is to decide that promises need not be kept with people who are wrong. A safe-conduct from an emperor was set aside and a man was burned on the strength of that reasoning. Christ's commendation of the church at Pergamos names a single man who died rather than deny, and names him in the middle of a city that killed him: “even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you” (Rev 2:13). The catalogue of faith lists the same end without softening it, “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder” (Heb 11:37).

pos: n. (the Rhineland town of the electors of Cologne, where Bucer's reforming order for the province was drafted in 1543)
etymology: From the Roman Bonna, a castrum on the Rhine, of Celtic or Germanic origin.
biblical_def: Bonn on the Rhine was a Roman garrison town and from the thirteenth century the residence of the archbishop-electors of Cologne, who preferred it to their quarrelsome cathedral city. It was therefore at Bonn, and not at Cologne, that Hermann von Wied worked on reforming his province: Martin Bucer was lodged there in 1542 and 1543 and with Melanchthon's help drew up the Einfaltigs Bedencken, the simple consideration, a reforming church order for the archbishopric which was published in 1543, translated into English in 1547, and used by Cranmer in drafting the first Prayer Book. The cathedral chapter and the Cologne theologians fought it, the archbishop was deposed, and Bonn was besieged and sacked in the Truchsessian war of 1583. The dictionary records Bonn for that document, which failed where it was written and succeeded in England. A church order is not a gospel, and the work it exists to serve is the plain one Paul gives Timothy: how to behave in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an order as regular disposition and rule; a house as a family and a place of worship; a pillar as a column supporting a building; truth as conformity to fact; and to behave as to conduct oneself.
webster_full: ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a rule or regulation; established mode of proceeding.
HOUSE, n. A building or edifice for the habitation of man; a family of ancestors and descendants; a place of worship.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated, used to support or adorn a building; a supporter.
TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
BEHAVE, v.t. To carry; to conduct; used with the reciprocal pronoun, to conduct one's self.
corruption_summary: Rhineland residence of the Cologne electors, where Bucer drafted the 1543 reforming church order that Cranmer later used for the English Prayer Book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that church order serves the church and never replaces it. Paul tells Timothy why he is writing at all, and the definition he gives of the congregation is the weightiest in the New Testament: “how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). What is to be kept is not a constitution but a shape of teaching: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13).

The live temptation when a reforming order fails is to conclude that the paper work was wasted, and Bucer's Bonn document was dead in Germany within four years and alive in England within five. The description Luke gives of the first congregation needs no document at all: they continued “daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house” (Act 2:46), and the increase was not theirs to arrange, for “the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved” (Act 2:47).

pos: n. (Charlemagne's capital and chapel, the coronation church of the German kings for six hundred years)
etymology: German Aachen, from the hot springs, Old High German aha, water; Latin Aquisgranum, French Aix-la-Chapelle.
biblical_def: Aachen in the far west of Germany was Charlemagne's chief residence, chosen for its hot springs, and he built there about 796 the octagonal palace chapel that still stands at the core of its cathedral, with columns brought from Ravenna and Rome. He was buried in it in 814. Thirty-one German kings were crowned at Aachen between 936 and 1531, and the chapel held the relics of Charlemagne and the so-called great relics, shown to pilgrims every seventh year. Alcuin ran the palace school there, Einhard wrote the emperor's life, and the Carolingian recovery of Latin learning was organised from the place. The city flirted with the Reformation, had a Protestant council in the 1580s, and was returned to Catholic rule in 1598 with its Protestants expelled. The dictionary records Aachen for the Carolingian school rather than the shrine. A court that gathered scholars from Northumbria, Italy, Spain and Ireland to copy and correct texts did more lasting good than every relic in the chapel, and it was done on the premise Paul states, that the teaching must be handed to men who can teach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; to copy as to write after an original; to correct as to set right; to commit as to entrust; and a chapel as a place of worship.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
COPY, v.t. To write, print or engrave according to an original; to form a like work by imitating an exemplar.
CORRECT, v.t. To make right; to rectify; to bring to the standard of truth, justice or propriety; to amend.
COMMIT, v.t. To give in trust; to put into the hands or power of another; to entrust; to consign.
CHAPEL, n. A house for worship, not being a parish church; a place of worship subordinate to another.
corruption_summary: Charlemagne's capital and burial place, whose palace chapel of about 796 crowned thirty-one German kings and whose palace school Alcuin directed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that made the Carolingian school fruitful and the shrine beside it barren, which is transmission to men who can teach again: what has been heard is to be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Christ redirects a blessing from a relic of his own flesh to the hearing and keeping of a word: “blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it” (Luk 11:28).

The live temptation at Aachen is the seventh-year showing of the great relics, a devotion built on objects rather than on obedience. James states the distinction in one clause: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jam 1:22). And the capacity a school depends on is not in its library: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9). Alcuin corrected texts at Aachen and the corrected texts outlived the empire that paid for them.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit as a trust; Greek phulasso (G5442), to keep; Greek poietes (G4163), a doer; Hebrew chakam (H2450), wise.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit as a deposit; “the same commit thou to faithful men”, 2 Timothy 2:2.

Greek poietes (G4163) — a doer, a performer; “be ye doers of the word”, James 1:22.
Greek paralogizomai (G3884) — to deceive by reasoning; “deceiving your own selves”, James 1:22.
Hebrew chakam (H2450) — wise, skilful; “Give instruction to a wise man”, Proverbs 9:9.
usage: “who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the palace school's premise.
“blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it” (Luk 11:28) — a blessing redirected.
“be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jam 1:22) — against the seventh-year showing.

But he said, Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.
Jam 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.

pos: n. (the Westphalian Hanse town whose law was copied across the north, and which reformed itself by civic ordinance in 1531)
etymology: Old Saxon Sosat, probably from a word for a salt spring or brine pit, the source of the town's early wealth.
biblical_def: Soest in Westphalia grew rich on salt and on the Hanse trade, and its municipal law, the Soester Schrae, was adopted by Lubeck and so passed to a hundred towns round the Baltic. It is built of a green local sandstone, and it kept more medieval churches than a town of its size has any right to. The Reformation came to it by town council: preaching began in 1531, the council issued a church ordinance that year drafted in consultation with Wittenberg, the mass was ended, and the town held its Lutheran settlement against its archbishop of Cologne thereafter, with a council of citizens and not a prince deciding the matter. The dictionary records Soest for that civic form of reform, which is neither a prince's decree nor a mob. A council of townsmen examined preaching, took advice, wrote an order and answered for it, and Scripture's instructions about truthful dealing and judgment in the gates are addressed to exactly that kind of body: speak every man the truth to his neighbour, and execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gate as the entrance of a city where judgment was given; judgment as the decision of a cause; a neighbour as one who lives near; lying as the utterance of falsehood; and upright as honest and just.
webster_full: GATE, n. A large door which gives entrance into a walled city, a castle, a temple or other inclosure; the frame which shuts it.
JUDGMENT, n. The act of judging; the act of determining, as in courts of law; the sentence or decision pronounced.
NEIGHBOR, n. One who lives near another; one who is entitled to kind offices; any one with whom we have dealings.
LYING, n. The act of uttering falsehood with an intention to deceive; the habit of telling lies.
UPRIGHT, a. Erect; perpendicular; honest; just; adhering to rectitude in all social intercourse.
corruption_summary: Westphalian Hanse and salt town whose municipal law spread round the Baltic, and which reformed itself by a civic church ordinance in 1531.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honest speech and honest judgment are public duties laid on the body that governs a town. Zechariah lists them together as things to be done: “Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates” (Zec 8:16). Paul gives the same command to a congregation and adds the reason, “speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another” (Eph 4:25).

The live temptation for a reforming council is expedience, a settlement arranged to suit the trade and defended with whatever argument serves. Solomon's standard admits no such latitude: “Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight” (Pro 12:22). And the man fit to stand in God's presence is described in terms a town council could be measured by, as one who “walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart” (Psa 15:2). Soest wrote an order and then had to live under it.

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon residence town of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, whose duke Ernest the Confessor brought in the Reformation in 1527)
etymology: From Middle Low German zelle, a cell or a settlement on a watercourse, from Latin cella.
biblical_def: Celle on the Aller in Lower Saxony was the residence of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg from 1378, a town of timbered houses round a castle with a chapel that was redecorated in the 1560s and is one of the best preserved Protestant princely chapels in Germany. Duke Ernest, who had been at the Diet of Worms and heard Luther, introduced the Reformation into his duchy from 1527 with a church order drafted by Urbanus Rhegius, visitations of every parish, and the founding of a school; he is called Ernest the Confessor for signing the protest at Speyer and the Augsburg Confession. The duchy kept its Lutheran settlement unbroken thereafter. The dictionary records Celle for the visitations, which are the unglamorous half of a reformation. Confessions are signed at diets; parishes are changed by somebody going to every village to find out whether the minister can preach and whether the children are taught. Scripture requires of stewards only that they be found faithful, and it says that faithfulness in a little thing is the test of faithfulness in much.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a steward as one entrusted with the management of another's affairs; faithful as firm in adherence to duty; least as the smallest; a servant as one who attends another; and joy as gladness and delight.
webster_full: STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns; one who is entrusted with the management of another's affairs.
FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to allegiance; constant in the performance of duties.
LEAST, a. Smallest; little beyond others, either in size or degree; the lowest in any scale.
SERVANT, n. A person who voluntarily serves another or acts as his minister; one who attends and obeys.
JOY, n. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness; exultation.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon residence town whose Duke Ernest the Confessor introduced the Reformation from 1527 with a church order, parish visitations and a school.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the work God actually requires of a servant is faithfulness and not scale. Paul reduces the whole job description to one clause: “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). Christ makes small things the diagnostic for large ones: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10).

The live temptation in a reformation is to measure it by diets, confessions and princes, and to find the parish visitation beneath notice. Celle's duke did both, signing at Speyer and at Augsburg and then sending men round every village. The commendation in the parable is given for exactly that second kind of work: “thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things” (Mat 25:21). The warning attached to it is against giving up before the harvest: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9).
